title: Keenen v. Russ
description: Whether the Energy Discrimination Elimination Act of 2022 (EDEA) is unconstitutional when applied to the Oklahoma Public Employees Retirement System (OPERS) because it conflicts with the Oklahoma Constitution's exclusive purpose clause for public retirement systems.
plaintiff_argument: Keenan argued the EDEA violated several provisions of the Oklahoma Constitution, including Art. XXIII, §12 (exclusive purpose for trust), by forcing OPERS to make investment decisions based on non-fiduciary purposes, potentially harming the retirement system.
defendant_argument: Treasurer argued Keenan lacked standing, and that the EDEA was designed to protect State funds by ensuring private entities managing those funds do not subordinate fiduciary duty to activist political goals, and that the Act makes providing benefits and investment management more effective.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the District Court's summary judgment, permanently enjoining the Treasurer from enforcing or applying the Energy Discrimination Elimination Act of 2022 to the Oklahoma Public Employees Retirement System.

title: Tobacco Settlement Endowment Trust Fund v. Stitt
description: Whether House Bill 2783, which changes the terms of the Tobacco Settlement Endowment Trust Fund (TSET) Board of Directors from fixed seven-year terms to at-will terms, violates the Oklahoma Constitution's requirement for fixed terms.
plaintiff_argument: The Tobacco Settlement Endowment Trust Fund (TSET) argued that HB 2783 is unconstitutional because it removes the constitutional requirement for TSET directors to serve staggered fixed seven-year terms.
defendant_argument: The respondents argued that HB 2783 preserves the fixed terms, that the Legislature has authority to create a removal mechanism, and that the Legislature has broad authority to alter appointment requirements if the Constitution is silent.
decision_outcome: The court found House Bill 2783 unconstitutional and granted declaratory relief, affirming that TSET directors must serve fixed seven-year terms as mandated by the Oklahoma Constitution.

title: White v. Stitt
description: Whether Senate Bill 632, which establishes business court divisions and an appointment process for judges, is constitutional under Article VII, Section 9 of the Oklahoma Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Senate Bill 632 is unconstitutional because it violates Article VII, Section 9 of the Oklahoma Constitution by circumventing the election of business court judges, and that they have standing as taxpayers and registered voters whose rights are infringed.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that Senate Bill 632 is constitutional, that business court judges are not district judges and thus not subject to election requirements, and that the plaintiffs lacked standing and he was not a proper party to the dispute.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that Senate Bill 632 is an unconstitutional violation of Article VII, Section 9 of the Oklahoma Constitution, voiding the Act in its entirety, and denied the Governor's Motion to Dismiss.

title: Donaldson v. City of El Reno
description: Whether applying current sex offender residency restrictions retroactively to an offender who became subject to the Sex Offenders Registration Act (SORA) before the law's enactment or amendment violates the ex post facto clause of the federal or state constitutions.
plaintiff_argument: Donaldson argued that applying the 2019 residency restrictions retroactively violates ex post facto laws, and the law in effect at his 2005 conviction, which did not prohibit residing near parks, should apply.
defendant_argument: The City of El Reno contended that the residency restrictions are nonpunitive, civil regulations, and therefore, their retroactive application does not violate the ex post facto clause.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's decision, ruling that the current residency restrictions for sex offenders do not constitute punishment and can be applied retroactively without violating ex post facto clauses.

title: Connor v. Oklahoma
description: Whether the Governmental Tort Claims Act's (GTCA) notice provisions apply to employment discrimination claims brought against a governmental entity under the Oklahoma Anti-Discrimination Act (OADA), with the plaintiff arguing they do not due to conflicts and the defendant arguing they do.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Claudia C. Conner, argued that the GTCA's notice provisions do not apply to her discrimination claims because the OADA covers intentional torts outside the scope of employment for GTCA purposes, and the OADA, as a more specific statute, should control over the GTCA due to material conflicts.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Oklahoma Employment Security Commission (OESC), argued that the plaintiff failed to comply with the GTCA's mandatory notice provisions, which are required for any cause of action against a governmental entity, and that there are no irreconcilable conflicts between the GTCA and OADA.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's denial of the OESC's motion to dismiss, holding that there are no material or irreconcilable conflicts between the GTCA and OADA regarding notice provisions, and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

title: Cherokee Nation  v. U.S. Department of the Interior
description: Whether the Attorney General of Oklahoma can assume control of the state's defense in a federal case, over the Governor's objection, when the Governor is a named defendant and has already retained counsel.
plaintiff_argument: The Attorney General argued that he has broad statutory authority to "take and assume control" of the state's defense in any litigation involving the state's interests, even over the Governor's objection.
defendant_argument: The Governor argued that he has specific statutory and constitutional authority, as the Chief Magistrate with "Supreme Executive power," to employ and direct his own counsel to protect the state's interests, and that the Attorney General's general authority does not supersede this.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the Attorney General cannot take and assume control of the state's defense in the federal case over the Governor's objection, where the Governor has lawfully retained his own counsel.

title: State v. Velasquez
description: Whether the Exclusionary Rule should be applied to suppress evidence obtained after a violation of the "knock and announce" rule (22 O.S.2021, § 1228) during the execution of a valid search warrant, with the State arguing against suppression and the Appellee arguing for it.
plaintiff_argument: The District Court abused its discretion by applying the Exclusionary Rule to suppress evidence for a violation of the "knock and announce" statute, arguing this remedy was too extreme and not warranted by the facts.
defendant_argument: The officers illegally executed a search warrant by violating the "knock and announce" rule, and therefore all evidence seized should be suppressed under the Exclusionary Rule.
decision_outcome: The State's appeal is GRANTED, the District Court's order granting the motion to quash the bindover is REVERSED, and the case is REMANDED for further proceedings consistent with the opinion.

title: Independent School District No. 12 v. State of Oklahoma
description: Whether the State Board of Education has the authority to control the selection of books in local school libraries, or if that discretion lies with local school boards based on local community standards.
plaintiff_argument: The State Board of Education lacks statutory authority to adopt and enforce library censorship rules, and the Governor's approval of these rules was improper, as local school boards have the discretion to select library content based on community standards.
defendant_argument: The State Board's rules were validly promulgated under its supervisory authority, the Governor's approval was legitimate, and the Attorney General's opinion to the contrary was incorrect, as the Board has the right to supervise local school library content.
decision_outcome: The court issued a writ of prohibition against the State Board of Education, State Department of Education, and State Superintendent of Public Instruction, directing them to dismiss enforcement proceedings against the Edmond School District regarding library book selection, but denied the petitioner's request for declaratory and injunctive relief.

title: Jackson County Emergency Medical Service District v. Kirkland
description: Whether the Jackson County Emergency Medical Services District (JCEMSD) is entitled to governmental immunity under the Governmental Tort Claims Act (GTCA) and if the GTCA precludes recovery for a plaintiff who has already received workers' compensation benefits.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the medical district is not a governmental entity and therefore not entitled to governmental immunity under the GTCA, meaning the GTCA's preclusion of recovery for workers' compensation recipients does not apply.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the JCEMSD is entitled to governmental immunity under the GTCA, and the GTCA precludes recovery because the plaintiff already received workers' compensation benefits.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court assumed original jurisdiction and granted the writ of prohibition, ruling that the medical district is subject to governmental immunity under the GTCA, and the lawsuit is precluded because workers' compensation benefits were already awarded.

title: Drummond  v. Statewide Virtual Charter Schoolboard
description: Whether the contract between the Oklahoma Statewide Virtual Charter School Board and St. Isidore of Seville Catholic Virtual School violates state and federal law and is unconstitutional, with the State arguing it does due to St. Isidore being a public charter school and thus a state actor, and the Charter School Board and St. Isidore arguing it does not as St. Isidore is a private entity and denying the contract violates the "no aid" provision or the Establishment Clause, and that denying the contract infringes on Free Exercise rights.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that St. Isidore, as a public charter school, is a governmental entity and state actor, and therefore, public funds cannot be used to establish or support a sectarian institution, violating the Oklahoma Constitution and the federal Establishment Clause.
defendant_argument: The Charter School Board and St. Isidore contend that St. Isidore is a private corporation, not a public school, and that the state's "no aid" provision does not apply. They also argue that denying St. Isidore the right to operate as a charter school solely due to its religious affiliation violates the Free Exercise Clause.
decision_outcome: The court ruled in favor of the State, granting the writ of mandamus and declaratory relief, finding the St. Isidore Contract violates state and federal law and is unconstitutional, and directed the Charter School Board to rescind the contract.

title: State Chamber of Oklahoma v. Cobbs
description: Whether Initiative Petition No. 446 is legally sufficient and constitutional to proceed to a vote by the people.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that Initiative Petition No. 446 is unconstitutional due to non-delegation doctrine violations, is not capable of correction by severance, and has a faulty gist, thus it should not proceed to a vote.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that Initiative Petition No. 446 is legally sufficient and does not clearly or manifestly violate the Oklahoma or United States Constitution, and therefore should be allowed to proceed to signature gathering and a vote.
decision_outcome: The court assumed original jurisdiction, denied all relief, and ruled that Initiative Petition No. 446 is legally sufficient and may proceed with signature gathering.

title: Deo v. Parish
description: Whether Oklahoma state courts have subject matter jurisdiction over crimes committed by an Indian in Indian Country, or if such jurisdiction is preempted by federal law, and whether the petitioner's claim was waived.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Billy Zane Deo, argued that the Okfuskee County District Court lacked subject matter jurisdiction over his cases because his crimes occurred in Indian Country and he is an enrolled member of the Muscogee Nation, citing McGirt v. Oklahoma.
defendant_argument: The defendant, The Honorable Lawrence Parish, implicitly argued that the state court retained jurisdiction, or that the petitioner's claim was waived due to his failure to raise it prior to entering his pleas.
decision_outcome: The court denied the Petitioner's application for an extraordinary writ of mandamus and remanded the matter to the Okfuskee County District Court for further proceedings.

title: Treat v. Stitt
description: Whether the Oklahoma Legislature's passage of S.B. 26x and H.B. 1005x, which extend State-Tribal compacts, is constitutional, specifically regarding the special session process, exceeding the session's call, and infringing on the Governor's authority to negotiate compacts.
plaintiff_argument: The Governor argued that the bills are invalid because they were passed during an unconstitutional concurrent special session, exceeded the scope of the special session's call, and infringed upon his exclusive constitutional and statutory authority to negotiate State-Tribal compacts.
defendant_argument: The Legislature contended that the concurrent special session was constitutional, the bills fell within the scope of the special session's call as they relate to budget-related funds, and the Governor's authority to negotiate compacts is statutory and subject to legislative limitation, not constitutional.
decision_outcome: The court denied the Governor's request for declaratory relief, upholding the validity of Senate Bill 26x and House Bill 1005x.

title: Oklahoma Call for Reproductive Justice v. Drummond
description: Whether three Oklahoma Acts (H.B. 1904, S.B. 778, and S.B. 779) that restrict abortion access are unconstitutional under the Oklahoma Constitution's due process clause, with plaintiffs arguing they place undue burdens on a woman's right to terminate a pregnancy to preserve her life, and defendants arguing they are designed to benefit women's health.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue that the three Acts severely and intentionally restrict access to abortions, place undue burdens on a woman's right to terminate her pregnancy to preserve her life, and are unrelated to patient health, thus violating the Oklahoma Constitution's due process clause.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that the three Acts are designed to benefit women's health and safety.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the trial court's order denying a temporary injunction, directed the trial court to grant a temporary injunction against the enforcement of H.B. 1904, S.B. 778, and S.B. 779, and remanded the matter for further proceedings on the merits.

title: Berkson v. State ex rel. Askins
description: Whether 28 O.S. § 86, which imposes a $10 Lengthy Trial Fund Fee on attorneys filing civil cases while exempting certain litigants, is an unconstitutional special law.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Berkson, argued that the Lengthy Trial Fund fee statute is an unconstitutional special law because it creates impermissible classes of similarly situated litigants by exempting pro se litigants without a logical connection to the likelihood of a lengthy trial.
defendant_argument: The defendants, the State of Oklahoma and District Court Clerks, argued that Berkson lacked standing to bring the action and that 28 O.S. § 86 is not an unconstitutional special law, as the legislative classification is reasonable.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the District Court's dismissal, concluding that the plaintiff's petition failed to state a claim that 28 O.S. § 86 is an unconstitutional special law.

title: Oklahoma Call for Reproductive Justice v. State
description: Whether Oklahoma's S.B. 1503 and H.B. 4327, which criminalize abortion, are constitutional under the Oklahoma Constitution, with petitioners arguing they are unconstitutional and the state arguing they are constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argued that S.B. 1503 and H.B. 4327 are unconstitutional as they prohibit abortion in violation of the Oklahoma Constitution, infringing on a pregnant woman's inherent right to terminate a pregnancy when necessary to preserve her life.
defendant_argument: The State of Oklahoma implicitly argued that S.B. 1503 and H.B. 4327 are constitutional and enforceable.
decision_outcome: The court assumed original jurisdiction, granted declaratory relief finding both S.B. 1503 and H.B. 4327 unconstitutional and unenforceable, but denied the petitioners' request for injunctive relief and writ of prohibition.

title: Schlumberger Tech. Corp. v. Paredes
description: Whether the statute of limitations for workers' compensation claims, as per 85A O.S.Supp. 2019, § 69 (A)(1), should be interpreted as "whichever is lesser" (Schlumberger) or "whichever is greater" (Paredes) when an employee has received benefits.
plaintiff_argument: Schlumberger argued that the statute should be interpreted as "whichever is lesser," meaning a claim is barred either one year from the date of injury or six months from the last benefit payment, whichever period is shorter, especially since the phrase "whichever is greater" was removed from the statute.
defendant_argument: Paredes argued that the statute should be interpreted as "whichever is greater," allowing the longer of the two periods (one year from injury or six months from last benefit payment) to avoid constitutional due process issues, particularly when the employer did not provide notice of the last benefit payment date.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Workers' Compensation Commission's order, ruling that Erasmo Paredes's claim was timely filed and not barred by the statute of limitations.

title: Oklahoma Call for Reproductive Justice v. Drummond
description: Whether the Oklahoma Constitution protects a right to terminate a pregnancy, and if so, whether state statutes criminalizing abortion (21 O.S. 2021, § 861 and 63 O.S.Supp. 2022, § 1-731.4) are constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argue that the Oklahoma Constitution protects a woman's right to terminate a pregnancy, making the challenged statutes criminalizing abortion unconstitutional as they violate inherent rights and substantive due process.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that the challenged statutes criminalizing abortion are constitutional and that the Oklahoma Constitution does not protect a right to terminate a pregnancy, especially an elective one, leaving such policy decisions to the state.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the Oklahoma Constitution protects a limited inherent right for a woman to terminate a pregnancy when necessary to preserve her life, finding 63 O.S.Supp. 2022, § 1-731.4 unconstitutional and unenforceable, but upholding 21 O.S. 2021, § 861 as constitutional due to its life-preserving exception.

title: MeGee v. El Patio, LLC
description: Whether dram shop liability should be extended to create a cause of action for a voluntarily intoxicated adult patron who is injured or dies as a result of his own intoxication, and whether a voluntarily intoxicated adult who accepts a bet to drive a motor vehicle and injures himself as a result of his own intoxication has a cause of action against the bettor.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that dram shop liability should be extended to cover injuries to voluntarily intoxicated adults, especially when employees over-served and then bet the intoxicated person to drive, creating a duty of care.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that Oklahoma law does not hold commercial vendors liable for injuries to voluntarily intoxicated adults due to their own intoxication, and 'negligent betting' is not a recognized theory of liability.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's dismissal, ruling that a voluntarily intoxicated adult has no cause of action against a commercial vendor for self-inflicted injuries due to intoxication, nor against a bettor who incentivized driving while intoxicated.

title: Kingfisher Wind, LLC v. Wehmuller
description: Whether Production Tax Credits (PTCs) utilized to finance the building of a wind farm are "property" which can be used to determine the fair cash value of the wind farm for ad valorem taxation purposes.
plaintiff_argument: Kingfisher Wind argues that PTCs are intangible personal property and are precluded from taxation by the Okla. Const. art 10, §6A.
defendant_argument: The County Assessors argue that PTCs are tangible personal property subject to taxation, as they provide an economic benefit to the wind farm and must be included in its fair cash value.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision, holding that Production Tax Credits (PTCs) are intangible personal property and are not subject to ad valorem taxation.

title: Ritter v. State
description: Whether Senate Bill 658, which restricts local school districts' ability to implement mask mandates without a gubernatorial emergency declaration, constitutes an unconstitutional delegation of legislative authority.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Senate Bill 658 was unconstitutional because it restricted local school districts' control over public health decisions, specifically mask mandates, and constituted an impermissible delegation of legislative authority.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that Senate Bill 658 was constitutional and enforceable, defending the state's authority to impose restrictions on local school districts regarding health measures.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the provision in Senate Bill 658 requiring a gubernatorial emergency declaration for local school districts to implement mask mandates was an unconstitutional delegation of legislative authority and struck that specific clause, upholding the remainder of the statutes.

title: Hudson v. State (In re K. H.)
description: Whether the trial court abused its discretion by admitting evidence of pending criminal child abuse charges and including them in jury instructions, thereby violating the parents' right to a fair trial in a parental rights termination case.
plaintiff_argument: The parents argued that the evidence of pending criminal child abuse charges was irrelevant, highly prejudicial, and violated their right to a fair trial, preventing a fair verdict.
defendant_argument: The State contended that the evidence of criminal charges was relevant to prove deprived adjudication and that its probative value outweighed any prejudice, and that the jury instructions mitigated any potential harm.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the District Court's judgment terminating parental rights and remanded the case for a new trial.
